newsitem.title: USA: Government wants one trial in Okla. City case.
newsitem.headline: Government wants one trial in Okla. City case.

text.p: Prosecutors in the Oklahoma City bombing case want only one trial for the two defendants, saying Timothy McVeigh and Terry Nichols were alleged to be co-conspirators and should be tried together, court records showed on Thursday.

"The deadly results of this conspiracy, as well as all the crime scene and forensic evidence, are admissible against both defendants," prosecutors wrote in a filing with the court on Wednesday that was made public Thursday.
McVeigh and Nichols, charged in the April 19, 1995, bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that claimed the lives of 168 people and injured hundreds more, both want separate trials.
Defence teams argued the strategy for the two defendants will be "antagonistic" and that defendants risk "spillover guilt" if put on trial together.
Next week U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch will hold a key pre-trial hearing on the defence motion for severance.

Prosecutors are anxious to try both defendants together, saying one trial would present a fuller picture of the bombing and spare what they called unnecessary suffering by the victims' and relatives of those killed.
The date for the Denver trial was not set, but was expected either late this year or early next.

Prosecutors said a single trial allows the case to be presented to jurors in its entirety. "While McVeigh actually delivered the bomb to the Murrah Building ... Nichols is charged both as a principal and as an aider and abetter of McVeigh," lawyers for the government said.

McVeigh's team was also concerned about statements Nichols made when he was questioned two days after the bombing, but prosecutors said the statements added little to what they called a "powerful case" against McVeigh.

Prosecutors also argued that case law did not establish a defendant's right to a separate trial because an "antagonistic" defence might result in each defendant pointing a finger of guilt at the other.
The Department of Justice lawyers also said that a defendant may be protected from any "spillover" prejudice by a proper instruction to jurors.
Statements by McVeigh about the conspiracy to commit the bombing should apply to Nichols because prosecutors will show that Nichols never withdrew from the conspiracy, government lawyers said.
Prosecutors also dismissed as unnecessary Nichols' lawyers' request that two juries be impaneled if one trial is held, but they said such a move would be preferable to holding two separate trials.
